note: Existing-source, strict-license-screened public gallery. Additional historical photos remain held from this site. Anatomy overlays are teaching annotations, not a separate verified voucher determination.

tiles.heading: 01 · FIND THE TRUE LIGULE
tiles.details: At the inner blade–sheath junction, inspect the torn-looking (lacerate) membranous ligule, about 0.5–2 mm long in Flora of North America; Kew GrassBase describes about 1 mm. Blades are commonly 2–4 mm wide, stiff and rough. Hairs behind the ligule are NOT the free ligule edge. An opened collar with millimeter scale is needed.
tiles.status: PUBLISHED COLLAR MEASUREMENT; PIXEL PROOF MISSING

tiles.heading: 02 · COUNT THE THREE-SPIKELET GROUPS
tiles.details: The compact terminal spikelike panicle is commonly 4–8 cm long and consists of repeated 5–8 mm fascicles. Each group carries ONE central fertile spikelet and TWO lateral predominantly staminate spikelets. These are THREE distinct spikelets, not three florets inside one spikelet. Detached groups may leave a zigzag axis shared with curlymesquite.
tiles.short: Dense terminal 4–8 cm head; triads 5–8 mm
tiles.status: HEAD PHOTO AVAILABLE; CALIBRATED FASCICLE MISSING

tiles.heading: 03 · OPEN THE CENTRAL FERTILE SPIKELET
tiles.details: Kew GrassBase describes the central fertile spikelet about 6–8 mm long, containing one bisexual fertile floret. Its glumes have divergent dorsal awns and lobed/fringed apices; the central lemma extends beyond the glumes and is bilobed, often mucronate. A Kew treatment describes a short ~1-mm lemma awn from the sinus; FNA emphasizes mucronate lemmas. Keep the literature distinction and do not label glume awns as lemma awns.
tiles.short: Central spikelet about 6–8 mm; lobed glumes
tiles.status: LITERATURE KEY; CENTRAL BRActs NOT DISSECTED

tiles.heading: 04 · INSPECT THE TWO LATERAL SPIKELETS
tiles.details: Two lateral male/staminate companion spikelets flank the central fertile one. Kew describes them as approximately 4–8 mm long, with 1–2 (occasionally more) staminate florets; FNA describes glumes as papery, lobed and fringed, with dorsal awns not exceeding the tips. Expose the lateral glumes and lemmas separately at 1-mm scale before drawing arrows; a whole fascicle photograph cannot prove bract insertion.
tiles.short: Male companions often 4–8 mm; glumes lobed

tiles.heading: 05 · TOBOSA OR CURLYMESQUITE?
tiles.details: Curlymesquite (H. belangeri) forms short turf with thin wiry ABOVEGROUND stolons rooting at hairy nodes; tobosa spreads by SHORT THICK SCALY UNDERGROUND rhizomes and is generally taller/coarser. Both bear three-spikelet fascicles and may leave zigzag axes. Vine mesquite has long aboveground runners with swollen nodes but lacks the same triad architecture. Do not use dry gray color or a solitary seedhead as species proof. Pleuraphis mutica is an alternative genus placement, not a second species.
tiles.short: Belowground scaly rhizome versus aboveground runner
tiles.status: LOCAL LOOK-ALIKES EXPLAINED; MATCHED ROOTS NEEDED

tiles.heading: 06 · OPTIONAL BELOWGROUND CONFIRMATION
tiles.details: Tobosa is a perennial forming tough coarse patches, with culms often 30–60 cm in Flora of North America. The decisive growth clue is a SHORT THICK SCALY RHIZOME BELOW SOIL attached to the culm, not an aboveground rooting stolon. The current photographs do not show a connected excavated rhizome; do not arrow a basal sheath as one.
tiles.short: Coarse perennial: expose the short scaly rhizome
tiles.status: BELOWGROUND RHIZOME IMAGE GAP — DEFERRED UNTIL ABOVEGROUND ANATOMY FINISHED

steps.title: 1 · First, recognize the plant
steps.look_for: TOBOSA / Hilaria mutica (also Pleuraphis mutica): FIRST photograph the TRUE inner 0.5–2 mm, torn-edged membranous ligule at the blade–sheath junction; note stiff 2–4 mm blades and short hairs on the blade just BEHIND the ligule. SECOND inspect attached dense 4–8 cm head of repeated 5–8 mm three-spikelet groups and, where possible, detached mature fascicles. Archived photographs prove whole flowering clusters and gross head structure, NOT the individual fertile central versus lateral staminate spikelets. Only LATER evaluate the short thick underground rhizomes to confirm against curlymesquite's surface stolons. Do not confuse the false ligule appearance of leaf hairs with the true membrane.
steps.why_it_matters: Start with the recorded recognition characters before making a species identification.

steps.title: 2 · Examine the whole plant
steps.look_for: First compare the real attached flowering-head views: Max Licher's pale fan-shaped lobes, Clifton Ladd's compact living head and Patrick Alexander's detached papery clusters. These show genuine broad structures, NOT confirmed separated central and lateral spikelets.
steps.why_it_matters: Habit and growing context are supporting evidence, not proof of hidden roots or rhizomes.

steps.title: 3 · Inspect leaves, collar and nodes
steps.look_for: At the inner blade–sheath junction, inspect the torn-looking (lacerate) membranous ligule, about 0.5–2 mm long in Flora of North America; Kew GrassBase describes about 1 mm. Blades are commonly 2–4 mm wide, stiff and rough. Hairs behind the ligule are NOT the free ligule edge. An opened collar with millimeter scale is needed.
steps.why_it_matters: Examine the real structures; the photo may not expose or measure all the described characters.

steps.title: 4 · Check the flowering structure
steps.look_for: The compact terminal spikelike panicle is commonly 4–8 cm long and consists of repeated 5–8 mm fascicles. Each group carries ONE central fertile spikelet and TWO lateral predominantly staminate spikelets. These are THREE distinct spikelets, not three florets inside one spikelet. Detached groups may leave a zigzag axis shared with curlymesquite.
steps.why_it_matters: Use an attached, correctly identified specimen when deciding the flower or spikelet structures.

steps.title: 5 · Compare similar grasses
steps.look_for: Curlymesquite (H. belangeri) forms a SHORT stoloniferous turf with aboveground runners and hairy rooting nodes, often 10–30 cm tall, whereas tobosa is generally taller/coarser and has BELOWGROUND thick scaly rhizomes, without stolons. Both can display triads of spikelets and residual zigzag axes. Vine mesquite (Hopia obtusa) has VERY LONG surface stolons with swollen hairy nodes rather than the tough short scaly tobosa rhizomes, and does not share tobosa's exact tightly triad-grouped spikelet structure.
steps.why_it_matters: Confirm at least two independent botanical characters; do not remove a native candidate from color alone.

panels.label: MATURE TOBOSA FASCICLES — real detached papery flowering groups (CC0)
panels.caption: Patrick Alexander's CC0 photograph of TOBOSA (= Pleuraphis mutica) shows several detached mature spikelet groups on the ground. Look at the radiating papery parts and tufts of hairs at their base. These are whole fascicles, NOT separate isolated glumes/lemmas, and the exact male vs fertile three-member positions are not proven without dissection. New Mexico locality, not a Texas voucher.
panels.creator: Patrick Alexander

panels.caption: Tobosa head photographed by Alex Abair in New Mexico. Follow the successive large, flared, paperlike and visibly parallel-veined pieces against blue sky. Do NOT label a particular visible part as central fertile glume, lateral male spikelet, lemma, or individual measured triad without a real dissection.

memory_rule: TOBOSA (sometimes Pleuraphis mutica): usually a tougher taller coarse perennial grass, commonly 30–70 cm in regional treatments, with compact spikelike head in groups of three spikelets, sometimes leaving a zigzag stalk after falling. Best confirmation is a SHORT THICK SCALY UNDERGROUND RHIZOME, NOT an aboveground surface stolon. Our real photograph shows a condensed fertile head and a coarse stiff dry-stand grass, but the attached scaly RHIZOME is absent; do not arrow sheath as rhizome.
safety_note: Twelve actual Tobosa photo records physically archived; 11 public eligible and 1 CC BY-NC private study hold. Public Learner panels include true same-species intact/veined/fanlike reproductive photos, an additional dark historic original USDA rhizome photo (only partial rootstock teaching quality), and separate correctly labelled Curlymesquite flowering/stolon comparisons. A visible true free lacerate 0.5–2mm membranous inner ligule and millimeter-scaled central bisexual plus lateral staminate spikelet dissection are still missing. Mobile/browser rendering QA pending.
field_rule: Recognize the compact repeated flowering units and stiff perennial habit first; confirm actual inner lacerate ligule and the three-spikelet fascicle before making an anatomical ID claim. Buried scaly rhizomes are a valuable later tiebreaker versus curlymesquite's surface stolons.
photo_data_caution: Missing or restricted comparison photographs have not been replaced by guesses. Source statements are not proof the associated structure is visible in any available photo.
